text: We now have two retrievers with opposite blind spots. Keyword search finds exact codes and names but misses paraphrases, while dense search finds paraphrases but blurs exact codes. Hybrid search runs both on every query and merges their results. The merging is harder than it sounds, because the two scores live on different scales: a BM25 score can be anywhere from zero to twenty or more, while a cosine similarity sits between minus one and one. Adding them directly is like adding rupees to kilometres.

The first remedy is to put both scores on a common scale before combining them. Min max normalisation does this per query: within each result list, the best score becomes one, the worst becomes zero, and everything else lands proportionally in between. Then the fused score is a weighted blend, alpha times the dense score plus one minus alpha times the keyword score, so alpha becomes a dial that slides between pure keyword search and pure semantic search.

The second remedy ignores the scores entirely and uses only the ranks. Reciprocal rank fusion gives each document one over sixty plus its rank in each list, and adds those up. A document ranked near the top by either retriever scores well, and one ranked well by both scores best. It needs no normalisation and no tuning, which makes it a robust default, but it discards how confident each retriever was, and that information is sometimes worth keeping.

To choose alpha, or to choose between the two methods, you need evidence rather than intuition, which means a set of real queries, each labelled with the passages that answer it. The usual measure is normalised discounted cumulative gain, or nDCG. Think of a theatre where the front rows matter most: a relevant passage earns credit that shrinks with the logarithm of its position, and dividing by the best possible ordering puts a perfect ranking at exactly one.

Now sweep alpha from zero to one, compute the average nDCG at each setting, and plot the curve. It usually rises to a peak somewhere in the middle, and where that peak sits depends on your queries: support tickets full of error codes lean towards keywords, while conversational questions lean towards meaning. With only a few dozen labelled queries the peak is noisy, so confirm the chosen value on a separate held out set before trusting it.

Production systems usually add one more stage, arranged like a funnel. The cheap retrievers cast a wide net, fetching perhaps a hundred candidates so that the right passage is very likely somewhere among them. A cross encoder, which reads the query and each candidate together, then reranks that short list carefully and keeps the best few. Filters on metadata, such as product or date, are applied before scoring, so that no effort is wasted on passages that could never qualify.

Retrieval has become a component you can measure and tune, rather than a black box you hope works. But it is only one part of the machinery that surrounds a model in a real application. The prompt has to be assembled, the reply has to be checked, and failures have to be handled gracefully. All of that together is called the harness, and it is the subject of the next lesson.
